title: The Boring Company & the Future Underground | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: An a16z Growth profile of the Boring Company (in which a16z invested at a $23B valuation) arguing that SpaceX-style first-principles engineering, vertical integration and automation have cut tunneling cost from ~$1B/mile to under $10M/mile, heading to $4-5M. Cheap tunnels plus point-to-point Teslas, privately funded stations and land-value capture could reshape urban transit, enable autonomy and hyperloop, and lower rents.

insights.claim: The Boring Company has cut tunneling cost below $10 million per mile since its 2017 founding, and CEO Steve Davis expects it to converge on $4-5 million per mile, which is already below the cost of adding an urban highway lane.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: A ~100x cost reduction vs. legacy urban tunneling reprices every underground infrastructure project; incumbents' bid economics look exposed.
insights.quote: If we’re below $5 million,” Davis asks, “why would you ever build a road again?
insights.locator: Since its founding in 2017

insights.claim: Legacy US urban tunneling benchmark: Los Angeles spent about $2 billion on a 2.5-mile subway extension, roughly $1 billion per mile, and spent $1.1 billion and five years adding a single 10-mile carpool lane to the I-405.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: The incumbent cost base the Boring Company attacks is enormous, so even partial cost gains open a large addressable market.
insights.locator: When TED’s Chris Anderson asked

insights.claim: Elon Musk's 10x tunneling cost plan had three levers: halve the tunnel diameter (12 ft vs. ~26 ft regulatory single-lane road tunnel) to cut cross-sectional area ~4x since cost scales with area; tunnel continuously instead of stopping to line walls (2x); and add power since machines are far from power/thermal limits (2x-5x).
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Cost reduction comes from compounding physical levers rather than one breakthrough, which makes the roadmap more credible.
insights.quote: Tunneling cost scales with the cross-sectional area,” Musk explains, “so that’s roughly half an order of magnitude right there.
insights.locator: His plan to make tunneling ten times cheaper

insights.claim: The Boring Company's original 1.14-mile Hawthorne test tunnel cost about $10 million all-in including the Godot machine, lighting, ventilation, safety systems and track, and the original 1.7-mile, three-station Las Vegas Convention Center Loop was built in about a year for roughly $47 million with no road closures.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Early projects established a verifiable cost base far below conventional transit.
insights.locator: In December 2018, Musk invited visitors

insights.claim: Boring Company stations cost from under $1 million up to $10 million for large ones, versus $250-500 million for a typical subway station, because point-to-point Loop stations can be as small as a few parking spaces.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Station cost collapse lets private landowners (even a taco shop) buy in, turning transit into a distributed private-capex model.
insights.locator: Another advantage of a point-to-point system

insights.claim: Nashville's Music City Loop first phase (about 10 miles from downtown to the airport) is put at roughly $200 million by the U.S. Department of Transportation, about $20 million per mile of route or $10 million per mile of tunnel, while the average American light rail line costs about eight times as much per route mile and takes about twice as long per mile to build.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Third-party (federal) cost figures validate the cost advantage vs. light rail in a hard-rock city.
insights.locator: Davis thinks about the project in terms

insights.claim: Tunneling in Nashville costs about half what it does in Las Vegas because the 14,000-psi limestone is stronger than the 8,000-psi concrete liner, letting the Boring Company use a simpler Prufrock Main Beam machine with no screw conveyor, grout, or concrete segments.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Geology can be an advantage rather than a cost penalty; hard-rock cities may be cheaper Loop markets than expected.
insights.quote: Nashville and the evolution of the planet has basically built the liner for us
insights.locator: The hard rock turned out to be a gift

insights.claim: Steve Davis argues that at $10 million per mile a pair of tunnels to a neighborhood 10 miles away costs $200 million versus $20 billion at the conventional $1 billion per mile, making suburban radial networks economically feasible.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Cost thresholds, not technology, gate network expansion; each cost step unlocks new route classes.
insights.locator: Las Vegas will be the first test

themes.theme: Musk's Algorithm applied to boring machines

insights.claim: Tunneling was dominated, like aerospace before SpaceX, by a few incumbents with cautious culture, little standardization and almost no incentive to cut costs: machines were custom-built per project by a handful of manufacturers mostly in Germany and China, and cost overruns were usually paid by the public.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Industries with cost-plus public funding and custom one-off hardware are ripe for SpaceX-style vertical-integration disruption.
insights.locator: Like the aerospace industry before SpaceX

insights.claim: The Boring Company dropped electric skates, car elevators, passenger pods and guide wheels as it applied the first steps of Musk's Algorithm (question every requirement, delete any part or process, simplify and optimize); critics called it backtracking, but the deletions cut cost and complexity, e.g. 'porpoising' machines dig their own ramp to the surface instead of using elevators.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Visible product 'retreats' can signal disciplined simplification rather than failure; judge on cost and throughput.
insights.locator: The electric skates from the TED video

insights.claim: Musk's deletion rule is that if you don't add back at least 10% of what you deleted, you didn't delete enough; the Boring Company cut trailing gantries from 14 to five and settled at six to eight.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: A concrete heuristic for aggressive simplification in hardware engineering orgs.
insights.quote: We deleted too much, which is classic.
insights.locator: The machine’s length got the same treatment

insights.claim: The Prufrock machine mines while building concrete rings by retracting some of its twelve hydraulic cylinders to place segments while the rest keep pushing, which took about two years to make safe and reliable and moved utilization from mining 5-10% of the time to more than 90%.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Continuous mining is the core technical moat behind the order-of-magnitude speed and cost claim.
insights.quote: I consider [building the concrete lining] to be a failure because you’re not pushing
insights.locator: The way a Prufrock machine works

insights.claim: Boring Company process fixes include cutting conveyor-belt splice time from eight hours to nine minutes via redesigned splice platforms and a 'fast splice' team, and launching machines off a tilting transporter called 'the Monster' instead of digging launch pits, saving millions per launch with the fastest launch going from empty site to mining in six and a half days.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Large gains come from attacking downtime and site prep, not just cutting speed.
insights.quote: Every time you stop, ask why
insights.locator: Dirt and muck are extracted

insights.claim: The Boring Company electrified tunnel logistics using Tesla parts: a battery-electric locomotive built from Model 3 motors and packs pulls a quarter million pounds of muck, removing diesel locomotives and their ventilation ducts.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Cross-Musk-company component reuse is a structural cost advantage competitors lack.
insights.locator: The team electrified everything else

insights.claim: The Boring Company's tunneling machines are already about five times faster than when Nashville started, and Steve Davis expects another tenfold gain; a minute shaved off each of 20,000+ five-foot pushes saves two weeks of schedule.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: If the projected 10x speed gain materializes, project timelines and costs fall further, widening the moat.
insights.locator: Davis thinks about the project in terms

themes.theme: Vertical integration and automation in Bastrop

insights.claim: The Boring Company's Bastrop, Texas factory (about 200 people, two shifts, seven days a week) builds a boring machine every two months and is working toward one per month; in-house part share rose from about 30% on Prufrock-1 to about 99% on Prufrock-6.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Near-total vertical integration and rising cadence mean fleet capacity, not machine supply, becomes the growth constraint.
insights.locator: Across the road is a 420-by-169-foot factory

insights.claim: Each Prufrock machine has roughly 176,000 parts and carries about a thousand design changes from its predecessor, so production lead Mike Baier calls them 'late-stage prototypes'; co-locating design engineers with machinists avoids routing cost/delay questions through three or four people at an outside shop.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Rapid iteration cadence resembles SpaceX/Tesla and implies a steep learning curve versus project-by-project incumbents.
insights.locator: Everyone works under the same roof

insights.claim: The Boring Company will not ship a machine until it has dug a test tunnel in Bastrop, a practice Davis borrowed from SpaceX's static fire, with subsystem designers operating the machine during tests.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Built-in test discipline reduces field failure risk, a key concern for city customers.
insights.quote: We’re the only company that I’m aware of that won’t ship a machine until it’s dug a test tunnel
insights.locator: A boring machine does not leave Bastrop

insights.claim: Boring Company crew size fell from about a dozen people on the first machine to two on the newest Prufrock; in May 2025 it demonstrated Zero-People-in-Tunnel (ZPIT) continuous mining, and by August 2026 ring building was fully autonomous, placing six ~3,750-pound segments with millimeter precision in under a minute.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Removing people also removes ventilation and safety-system overhead, a compounding cost reduction; zero-crew would let it 'unleash a fleet'.
insights.quote: Getting to two is hard, but not that hard
insights.locator: Boring’s first machine needed about a dozen

insights.claim: All Boring Company machines are run from a Global Operations Control Center (GOCC) in Texas; each machine carries about 80 cameras and over 1,700 sensors, and every subprocess is remote-controlled before being automated so automation always has a graceful human fallback.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Teleoperate-then-automate is a pragmatic path to autonomy in industrial robotics that de-risks deployment.
insights.locator: All of it is operated from the company’s Global

themes.theme: Loop product, network effects and private-capture business model

insights.claim: The Vegas Loop has carried more than four million passengers since 2021, has 29 stations and over 10 miles of tunnel, demonstrated peak capacity above 4,500 passengers an hour and 32,000 a day, and local officials have approved 68 miles of tunnel and 123 stations.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Approved pipeline is ~6-7x the current network, giving visible growth runway in the home market.
insights.locator: Tunneling began on November 15, 2019

insights.claim: The Loop's point-to-point, non-stop design means adding stations does not slow trips: Davis estimates a train stopping at every hotel would take about 90 minutes end to end of the Las Vegas Strip, versus about eight minutes on Loop regardless of station count.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Point-to-point topology breaks the subway trade-off between coverage and speed, enabling dense networks.
insights.quote: There’s only two ways to solve the problem,” Davis says. “You don’t stop, or if you’re willing to stop, you can’t have that many stations.
insights.locator: Vegas was the ideal proving ground

insights.claim: The Boring Company flips the US transit funding model: property owners pay for their own stations, riders pay fares about half the price of a rideshare or less, the company buys land along routes to capture value its tunnels create, and it asks for no taxpayer dollars, echoing developer-funded streetcars a century ago.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Value capture via land ownership could make the company part real-estate play, with upside beyond fare revenue.
insights.quote: We don’t ask for any taxpayer dollars
insights.locator: The business model was another area

insights.claim: Loop has network effects: each new station adds destinations for riders and gives property owners another reason to join, and Resorts World saw demand rise about 30% after opening its Loop station in 2022; several customers say they will open a station once 20 others are open.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Network-effect dynamics imply accelerating adoption as tunnel miles grow, favoring the scaled incumbent.
insights.quote: the system’s usefulness is limited by the number of tunnel miles we have and are open
insights.locator: There are also network effects

insights.claim: In its Las Vegas deal the Boring Company bid about $52.5 million, roughly a quarter of Doppelmayr's original above-ground people-mover estimate, and assumed financial risk by having two-thirds of payment held back until the system worked, with a full refund if it never got a certificate of occupancy.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
entities: Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority
insights.so_what: Risk-transfer contracting lowered the barrier for a first municipal customer and is a replicable go-to-market tactic.
insights.locator: Las Vegas was different

insights.claim: Ride-experience engineering raised Loop throughput: Davis chose Model Ys after timing riders exiting two to three seconds faster than from a Model 3, and asking riders to leave doors open raised capacity 10-15%.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Capacity is an operations problem; small UX gains compound into material throughput.
insights.quote: Capacity is driven by how fast you can load and unload
insights.locator: Davis treats the ride experience

insights.claim: The Boring Company's early projects in Chicago (O'Hare link), Washington-Baltimore and Los Angeles stalled due to politics, federal environmental review and a lawsuit over a single test tunnel; Musk called L.A. 'one of the worst places to dig tunnels, mostly because of the paperwork.'
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Regulatory jurisdiction choice matters more than technology for infrastructure start-ups; avoid high-friction permitting regimes.
insights.quote: Nobody is set up to permit Loop, because how could they be?
insights.locator: Elsewhere, Boring’s plans got buried

insights.claim: Permitting is getting easier for the Boring Company: the Las Vegas system needs more than 600 permits, whereas the entire Nashville project was permitted in one shot, and the company began tunneling the same day it received its Tennessee DOT permit on February 25, 2026.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: A working reference project de-risks the 'yes' for each subsequent city, so expansion should accelerate.
insights.quote: the entire thing was permitted in one shot
insights.locator: Each new city should be easier

insights.claim: The Boring Company announced a $3 billion Series D at a $23 billion valuation in September 2026, in which a16z participated.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Private-market marks a tunneling company at $23B; the authors are investors, so treat the profile as bullish-biased.
insights.locator: In September, the company announced

insights.claim: Davis predicts the first mile of Nashville's Music City Loop, covering the convention center and four major properties, will carry passengers in Q1 of next year, with all 22 miles of tunnel finished in two to three years.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: A near-term, checkable milestone for tracking execution on the second-city rollout.
insights.locator: Davis thinks about the project in terms

insights.claim: Internationally, the Boring Company signed a construction contract with Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority for a ~4-mile, four-station Dubai Loop pilot cutting the financial-district-to-Dubai Mall trip from 20 to three minutes, with tunneling planned for late 2026 under a broader UAE partnership of more than 150 km of tunnel.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Gulf demand provides a large, permit-friendly international growth vector.
insights.locator: Internationally, the company signed

insights.claim: The Boring Company's US pipeline also includes Dallas and New Orleans as Tunnel Vision Challenge winners (a free one-mile tunnel), Orlando in early approvals, San Antonio, and a Cybertunnel moving Cybertrucks from Tesla's Austin Gigafactory under an eight-lane highway in about a minute.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Multiple city entry points signal a broadening customer base beyond Las Vegas.
insights.locator: Closer to home, Dallas and New Orleans

insights.claim: The Boring Company was spun out of SpaceX in early 2018 and raised $112.5 million in April 2018, about 90% from Musk; before that, merchandise was its only revenue, including 20,000 'Not a Flamethrower' units at $500 that sold out in four days for $10 million.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Founder-funded, merch-bootstrapped origins show capital efficiency before institutional rounds.
insights.locator: With bids in Washington, Los Angeles, and Chicago

themes.theme: Autonomy, hyperloop and land-value second-order effects

insights.claim: Elon Musk argues self-driving cars will make tunnels more necessary, not less, because once shared autonomous rides are cheaper than a bus, total driving will rise sharply and traffic will get far worse.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Robotaxi adoption could be a demand tailwind for tunnel capacity rather than a substitute.
insights.quote: the amount of driving that will occur will be much greater, and traffic will get far worse.
insights.locator: Musk also argued that self-driving cars

insights.claim: Musk claims tunnels escape the induced-demand trap that makes driving rise roughly one-for-one with new highway lanes, because tunnel lanes can be added faster than demand grows, with 'hundreds of levels' possible.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: If true, tunnels avoid the core failure mode of road expansion; skeptical investors should test this against real congestion data.
insights.quote: You could have hundreds of lanes,” he says, “and there’s no real limit.
insights.locator: What about induced demand?

insights.claim: Already 5-10% of Loop rides run without a driver; the authors argue a sealed one-way tunnel with no pedestrians, cross traffic, weather or left turns is the friendliest environment for autonomous cars, and Davis envisions a station in every driveway with robotaxis dropping into nearby portals.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Tunnels are a constrained-domain shortcut to autonomy, linking Boring's value to robotaxi economics.
insights.locator: “Tunnels under cities with self-driving

insights.claim: The a16z authors argue autonomous cars plus tunnels is the most promising way to reduce road deaths, since car crashes kill more than a million people a year worldwide and are the leading cause of death for children and young adults; the Loop has carried over 4 million passengers without a passenger-related safety or security incident.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Safety record is a key regulatory unlock for scaling underground autonomous transit.
insights.locator: A city like that would also be far safer

insights.claim: The Boring Company's vacuum test of a sealed tunnel showed pressure can easily go below 1 psi (struggling near 0.5), versus 7-10 psi needed for very high speeds and 14.7 psi at sea level, with an acceptable leak rate, supporting a hyperloop path; Musk says a >200 mph precursor tunnel between Austin and San Antonio could cut a 2.5-hour trip to under 30 minutes.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Hyperloop optionality is a long-dated call option embedded in the valuation, with execution rather than physics as the stated risk.
insights.quote: Most of the risk is us executing, which is great from the hyperloop perspective.
insights.locator: Then, once tunnels are cheap

insights.claim: Davis argues the biggest benefit of cheap tunnels is lowering urban rent: shortening a two-hour commute to ten minutes turns cheap remote land into land near everything; Boring plans a 132-unit apartment building with a ground-floor Loop station a mile from the Strip, and developers are considering projects 10-20 miles from urban cores.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Second-order winner is peripheral land and transit-oriented real estate; Boring's own land purchases position it to capture this.
insights.quote: You can solve the rent and cost of living problem by making all of these places very desirable to live with just transportation
insights.locator: The most important consequence of this underground

insights.claim: By the Boring Company's estimate, roads take up 20-30% of land in many major cities and up to 60% including parking, so moving traffic and utilities underground could free large amounts of urban land.
insights.speaker: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
insights.so_what: Land freed from roads/parking is a large latent value pool for cities and developers.
insights.locator: Moving traffic underground also frees up land

source_meta.author: David George, Jamie Sullivan, Michael McGuiness
